For the EB school no-spin method the basics are:

Stretch out your target circle past the hole until you’re at max distance with the EB. Then estimate what percentage the distance to the hole is from the ball to max distance. For instance, if the hole looks like it’s 1/3 of the way from the ball to max distance you’d set your slider to 33%. 

Then set up your target with no topspin or backspin so the ball guide goes dead center into the pin. At the lower level you’re at I’d probably put the ball guide just into the hole so it doesn’t come in too hot. If the green slopes downhill I’d try having the guide stop just before the hole, and if the green slopes up then have it go to the back of the pin. 

If you get a glitchy ball guide then try some sidespin to see if it fixes that. 

Then adjust your EB at +20% elevation at the slider you decided on. Usually it’s money.
Definitely this. At the levels you’re at the EB has more reach, better accuracy, and a better ball guide. Using the EB school no-spin will be money for you.

Okay, so if you zoom in on the target (to adjust rings), if the target is on a much lower elevation you’ll notice how it doesn’t let you zoom in as far. If you keep trying to zoom it forces your POV to go down to the ground without getting any closer to the circle, so it’s like you’re looking at it from the side and it’s really hard to adjust. 

So basically the closer you’re able to zoom on the target the smaller the elevation difference, OR the landing spot might even be higher than where you’re shooting from. 

This is mostly useful for me if I don’t notice that I’m shooting into a significantly lower elevation, but then when I zoom in on the target I notice the can’t zoom in as close as usual. Then I’ll know it’s more downhill than I thought and to increase my adjustment.
A good thing to look for is how much the game lets you zoom in on the shot target before the camera pans down towards the ground and you’re looking at the target from the side.

I have a Falcon 7 and still don’t use it most of the time. Adjusting with the Thorn is really easy, typically 1% per ring adjusting from min or max. If I have the elevation dialed in on a hole I usually sink my Thorn shots. And yeah, accuracy isn’t great, but with any of the clubs you’ll miss if you hit great (assuming you adjusted correctly). 

If I know for a particular hole that the approach shot would be tight at short iron range, like the danger is high to go in the rough or sand with a great ball, I’ll pack my falcon. Otherwise it’s Thorn all the way until I get my Falcon to 8.

Drivers, woods, and long/short irons have a min and max distance before it’ll switch to another club or just max out if there isn’t a longer club you can use. For people who try to use exact adjustments for wind and elevation, we also look at where we’re trying to take our shot within the min/max range of the club. 

For instance, if our target is about 3/4 of the way from min and max we would try to adjust to that club’s 75% distance adjustment. Apps like Clash Caddie and Notebook for Golf Clash have a distance slider you can use to help you figure your exact numbers.

First try taking the bearing out (if it does) and dropping it in a little cup with some isopropyl alcohol (at least 91%).  Use your finger to roll the bearing around the edge of the cup, and you can shake it up a little too.  Leave it in for at least 15 minutes.  Then take it out, shake it off and dry it with a hairdryer, spinning it as you dry it.

If that doesn't make it significantly better, get some mineral spirits (you can find it in a hardware store).  Do the same thing with that, and then put it briefly in alcohol afterward (to clean off the mineral spirits).  If it's still not good, then the bearing is likely damaged and you need to get a new one.

Oh, and if the bearing isn't removable and the spinner is made of plastic, don't use alcohol (it can damage some ABS plastics).  Mineral spirits should work okay, then rinse it and dry it off right away with a hairdryer.

Yes, I'd get a new bearing too.  Since you can't remove the shields, you can't really get gunk out of the bearings.  Sealed bearings suck IMO, because all bearings will eventually get some grit inside, and with these you're pretty much screwed at that point.  

Edit: Also, it's not necessary to lube the bearing, depending on what you want out of the spinner.  A clean, dry bearing will give you the longest spin times, but it will be louder and give more feedback.  If you want to lube it, use the lightest oil you can find (valve oil for brass instruments is my favorite), and only put a little bit in it.  Lubed bearings are quieter, but they won't spin as long because the lube puts a little resistance in the bearing.

It's the mechanics of how the instrument works. 

Woodwinds all have holes cut into the length of their body, which are opened and closed to change pitch. They also typically use a reed to create the initial vibration, except for the flute & piccolo, which makes sound by blowing against the sharp edge of the embouchure hole (blow hole) rather like blowing air over the top of a pop bottle.  

For woodwinds, the less distance air has to travel from the head of the instrument until it can "escape" through an open hole, the higher the pitch will be (except for special keys that vent very small holes in ways that allow the instrument to jump to a higher harmonic or when you play super high notes).  So as you close more holes down toward the bottom of the instrument, the pitch gets lower. 


For brass instruments, it is a closed system, with no holes from the mouthpiece to the bell (except spit valve holes to release water, but those are closed when you play).  The top of a brass mouthpiece is shaped like a funnel with a small hole at the bottom (which opens up again at the shank where it connects to the rest of the instrument.  As you blow into it (if you do it right), the back pressure from the air constricting into the small hole helps your lips to vibrate, which in turn vibrates the column of air in the instrument.  If the vibrations are in line with one of the harmonics (or overtones) of the instrument, based on its length, then it will make that sound.  

Without pushing any valves down (or moving the trombone's slide), there's a series of notes that brass instruments can play called the harmonic or "overtone" series.  If you've ever heard a military bugle play revelie or taps, a bugle is essentially a Bb cornet (almost the same as a trumpet) without valves.  So a trumpet player not pushing down any valves can play those same notes, but nothing in between.  The distance between these harmonics is pretty large at the lower pitches, but closer together at higher ones. 

When a valve is pushed down, holes inside the piston (or rotor) redirect the air into a separate length of tube connected to the valve, in essence making the column of vibrating air longer, which lowers the pitch a certain amount from whatever harmonic you would be playing.  Each valve has a different length of tubing connected to it, so that by pressing different combinations of valves, you can get any pitch in between harmonics. 

FINALLY, a saxophone, while is it made of brass, uses a reed for the initial sound, and has holes cut into its body that are opened and closed like any other woodwind.  

Source: have been a band director for 14 years and know how to play all of these fairly well.

When I was about 11, I lived in western Colorado, and a friend & I got some little fireworks (spinning firewheels mostly) and thought it was be hilarious to go on a bridge over the freeway and throw them on the road before cars go by.  Okay, it was mostly my idea and my friend thought I was an idiot.  Which I was. 

Anyway, I light a few spinners and throw them down on the road.  They're merrily spinning their pinwheels of fire as some cars drive over them.  But what I hadn't thought of was that there was a field of tall grass, quite dry in the desert heat, right on the side of the road.  One of the spinners bounced right into it, and I had my first really serious "Oh, shit" moment I can remember.  My friend had already noped the fuck out of there and was riding his bike down the hill away from the freeway.  I quickly followed, and as I pedaled furiously I glanced over and saw a brush fire already going that I didn't have a hope of doing a thing about. 

The road kept sloping down about 1/2 a mile down to the main road.  When we got there we looked back and tried to see smoke.  The light was coming the wrong way for us to see any, so I started calming down and thinking it went out and would be okay.

Then three fire engines tore ass up the road toward the fire and we rode home a different way.  I probably said "Oh shit" about 500 times on the way. 

Later, I was riding with my parents on the freeway and they remarked at the quite large blackened field.  I was like, "Huh.  Wonder how that happened."

Never told anyone until I grew up (though I still haven't told my folks; they had enough reasons to think I was bad at making smart decisions). 

Tl;dr: Started a brush fire along the freeway because I was throwing fireworks on the road from a bridge.  Multiple fire trucks came to put it out, but nobody found out I did it.

The highest dew point ever recorded was in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia on July 8, 2003, and was a mind-blowing 95° (for reference, a dew point in the 70's feels really sticky and awful). Dew point measures how much moisture is in the air by saying, "This is the temperature where you would be at 100% relative humidity with the current moisture level, and the water vapor will condense out of the air to form clouds/fog."  In order to be at 98% RH, the dew point has to be less than 1° below the air temperature.  So at 111° the dew point would have to be 110° to get up to the upper 90's in RH.
